subject: Art & Design
title: How Light Creates Color
description: A quick, practical guide to How Light Creates Color.

hook.text: A red apple isn't red. It absorbs every wavelength except red, which it reflects to your eyes.

buildup.text: White light contains all visible wavelengths. Objects selectively absorb and reflect them.

discovery.text: This is why the same shirt looks different under fluorescent light vs. sunlight — the light changes.

twist.text: There's no color in the physical world. Color exists only in the brain's interpretation of light.

climax.text: Metamerism: two colors that match under one light can look completely different under another.

punchline.text: Color isn't in objects. It's in the light bouncing off them.

quiz.question: Why does a red apple appear red?
options: It absorbs all wavelengths except red, which it reflects
It generates red light from within
Our eyes always add red to round objects

details.summary: Color doesn't exist in objects — it's created by light. When white light hits an apple, the surface absorbs all wavelengths except red, which reflects to our eyes. Different light sources have different spectra, which is why colors look different under fluorescent, incandescent, and natural light.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding that color is light-dependent prevents costly errors in design, fashion, and interior decoration. A paint color chosen under store fluorescents can look entirely different at home under warm bulbs — a phenomenon called metamerism.
takeaways: Color is reflected light, not an inherent property of objects
Different light sources make the same color look different
Metamerism explains color shifts between lighting conditions

faq.question: What is metamerism and why does it matter?
faq.answer: Metamerism occurs when two colors appear identical under one light source but different under another. Two fabric samples might match perfectly in a store but clash in natural daylight. Designers check colors under multiple light sources to prevent metamerism surprises.

faq.question: Why do things look different colors at sunset?
faq.answer: Sunlight at sunset passes through more atmosphere, which scatters blue wavelengths and allows red and orange wavelengths to dominate. Objects are illuminated by warm-biased light, shifting all colors warmer. Blues appear muted, reds appear intensified — the same physics that creates the red sky.
